introduction.p: The Taylor polynomial at a matches a function's value and derivatives through a chosen order. Its first-degree case is the tangent-line approximation f(a)+f\prime(a)(x-a). Higher degrees incorporate higher derivatives. The next section will bound the remainder.

exercise.title: Why does a Taylor polynomial match derivatives at a center?

statement.p: The tangent line matches value and slope. A Taylor polynomial continues the matching through higher derivatives. In your own words, why is that the right way to build a local polynomial, and what local information is each extra coefficient recording?

hint.p: Near a point, the first things a smooth function reveals are its value, its rate of change, its bending, and so on. Matching those derivatives makes the polynomial share the function’s local shape.

exercise.title: What is each Taylor term doing?

statement.p: For \sqrt{1+x} near 0, the linear term follows the tangent, the quadratic term corrects for concavity, and the cubic term corrects the correction. In your own words, why is a Taylor polynomial not just a formula, and why do later terms matter less when you stay close to the center?

hint.p: Each coefficient is derivative data at one point. Close to the center, higher powers of x-a are small, so the first few matched derivatives dominate the picture.

paragraphs.title: A necessary warning
paragraphs.p: Taylor polynomials require derivatives at the center.
The function
is continuous at 0, but it is not differentiable at 0. The left slope is -1, and the right slope is 1. There is no single number f'(0).
So there is no first-degree Taylor polynomial for |x| centered at 0 that matches the derivative. The needed local data does not exist.

note.title: Moral
note.p: A Taylor polynomial is built from derivatives at a center. If those derivatives do not exist, the polynomial cannot be built in the usual way.

paragraphs.p: There is another warning. Even when the polynomial exists, it is only a local approximation until we understand its error.
For e^x, the polynomial
approximates the function near zero under the relevant remainder estimate. Matching derivatives at one point alone gives no accuracy bound far from that point.
That is the next question:

p.me: \text{How far is \(f(x)\) from its Taylor polynomial?}

paragraphs.p: The answer is the remainder term. Without it, approximation has no scale.

exercise.title: What does a Taylor polynomial match at its center?

statement.p: Taylor polynomials require derivatives at the center, and even when they exist they are not automatically accurate far away. In your own words, why can |x| have no first-degree Taylor polynomial at 0, and why is matching at a point not yet a statement about error on an interval?

hint.p: Without a derivative, there is no slope to match. With a derivative, contact at a point still says nothing about how large the leftover gap becomes as you move away. That gap is the remainder.
